newsitem.title: USA: Crime beginning to threaten New Orleans' tourism.
newsitem.headline: Crime beginning to threaten New Orleans' tourism.

text.p: A national poll showing crime threatens the level of tourism in New Orleans was released just hours after a Kentucky tourist was gunned down in the French Quarter during a robbery attempt Monday.
The New Orleans Metropolitan Convention and Visitors Bureau ordered the Gallup poll in 1996 to find out why bookings for future meetings in the city were decreasing, spokeswoman Beverly Gianna said.

Nine hours earlier, Terry Keiser, 38, of Taylor Mill, Kentucky, died as he and another conventioneer walked to their hotel from Pat O'Brien's nightclub. A man jumped from a car, demanded money and then opened fire, hitting Keiser just below the left eye, police said.

The Gallup survey indicated crime has not had a significant impact on the city's tourism business, but it suggested convention organisers were beginning to view New Orleans as unsafe and dirty when compared to regional competitors like San Antonio, Atlanta and Dallas.
"We've got some realy dark clouds on the horizon, things that we have to look at and address," said Tim Ryan, dean of the Universty of New Orleans College of Business Administration.
For the survey, Gallup telephoned 562 meeting planners whose names were provided by the Convention and Visitors bureau.

Planners ranked New Orleans first as a convention site, ahead of San Francisco, Chicago and Orlando, but 52 percent cited crime as the "least positive aspect of holding events in new Orleans." Eight percent cited dirtiness of the city as a negative.

Annually, an estimated nine million tourists visit New Orleans, many of them with conventions. The toursim industry accounts for one in six jobs in the city and $1 of every $14 of wages paid, according to MetroVision, a regional promotion group.

Bill Langkopp, executive vice president of the Greater New Orleans Hotel/Motel Association, called crime the industry's "Achilles' heel." Of Keiser's death, he said, "We've got to recognise that a person died, that it's a real human tragedy" that could have grave financial repercussions for the city."
